A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Threshold Differential Attention study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-modeling, SCROLLS, passkey retrieval, mechanistic, hyperparameter and kernel-efficiency results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds multi-needle retrieval, BF16 kernel benchmarks and empirical diagnostics of the theoretical assumptions.

M1.justification: The normalized query/key scores, length-dependent threshold, powered rectification, differential subtraction and output normalization are unchanged. The forward/backward pseudocode is also retained; the added evaluations do not establish an algorithm or implementation change.

E1.justification: Section 6.4 adds retrieval of two or four key-value pairs from widely separated positions, extending the original single-passkey task requirements. FineWebEdu training, the six standard benchmarks and four SCROLLS tasks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: FlashAttention-2 becomes an actually evaluated comparator in the new BF16 efficiency benchmark, whereas v1's efficiency comparisons used dense Softmax, naive TRA and fused SDPA. Those FP32 comparisons and the comparator sets in Tables 2–3 are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds a separate BF16 latency protocol spanning 512–65,536 tokens with matched hardware and tensor layouts, alongside the retained FP32 benchmark. New protocols also cover multi-needle accuracy, survivor counts at lengths 256–2048 and trained/untrained correlation controls. Existing training settings and benchmark protocols are unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix B investigates logit tails, relevant-token survivor scaling and cross-view correlation to examine the theoretical assumptions. Section 6.4 additionally tests whether extreme sparsity harms retrieval from multiple distant locations. Existing mechanistic analyses and power/threshold ablations are retained.

E5.justification: The new BF16 benchmark specifies median latency reporting, and Appendix B explains that undefined correlations are excluded from layer averages. Both versions retain seed 1337 and single-run evaluation reporting; no confidence intervals, significance tests or explicit increase in training runs is introduced.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include 82% TDA versus 0% Softmax accuracy for two needles at 4000 tokens, and BF16 latency of 24.641 ms for TRA versus 31.713 ms for FlashAttention-2 at 32,768 tokens. Appendix B adds diagnostic results. Earlier numerical results are retained; these additions are separate experiments, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The formal assumptions, definitions, survivor bounds, non-dispersion results and Appendix A proofs are unchanged. Appendix B supplies empirical diagnostics rather than new mathematical guarantees; the changed theorem/corollary wording in an appendix heading does not revise the mathematics.

C1.justification: The introduction's efficiency contribution shifts from FP32 memory/runtime advantages over SDPA to TRA's BF16 competitiveness and long-context speedups against FlashAttention-2. The central sink-free, ultra-sparse, non-dispersive and competitive language-modeling claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of the assumptions through empirical diagnostics, explicitly treating them as approximate support rather than verification. It interprets multi-needle results as preserving distant interactions and attributes BF16 gains to reduced value aggregation. Limitations further qualify large-model sparsity, stability and efficiency, and discuss inactive heads as possible idle states.

D1.justification: v2 adds CUDA-event timing information and diagnostic processing details, including excluding padding from survivor counts and undefined correlations from averages. The code access link, pseudocode, training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain unchanged. These are documentation additions, not evidence of changed training implementation.

R1.justification: The bibliography and related-work discussion are retained. Research positioning changes locally: the introduction and Section 6.5 now explicitly position the TRA kernel as competitive with FlashAttention-2 under BF16, beyond v1's discussion of FlashAttention-inspired streaming and FP32 comparisons.

P1.justification: v2 adds two experimental subsections and Appendix B, expands the limitations and revises the efficiency contribution. Subsequent sections and appendices are renumbered, but most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Three new tables—multi-needle retrieval, BF16 latency and logit tails—and two diagnostic plots substantially expand the empirical displays. Existing figures are retained unchanged, while tables and floats are relocated. The hyperparameter table also corrects best-loss highlighting without changing its numerical values.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's FP32-only efficiency evidence, v2 provides a more practically relevant BF16 comparison with FlashAttention-2 and useful tests of multi-location retrieval and theoretical assumptions. These strengthen support for the paper, but the new protocols are briefly specified and the assumption diagnostics remain indirect. The central method and main language-modeling evidence are unchanged.
